newsitem.title: USA: US debt futures end down on talk of big 10-yr sale.
newsitem.headline: US debt futures end down on talk of big 10-yr sale.

text.p: U.S. debt futures finished a choppy session moderately lower Wednesday after a late slide that traders said was triggered in part by talk of a large sale of 10-year cash Treasurys.
A dealer firm was said to have sold at least $1 billion worth of 10-year notes, floor traders said.

Traders also linked the late selling to concern about rising oil prices after OPEC oil ministers agreed to freeze production quotas at talks being held in Vienna, and pointed a finger at comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that they characterized as unsettling.
Rubin said that while there was no reason to expect concerted selling of U.S. Treasury securities, financial markets are big enough to absorb such selling if it were to occur.

September bond futures staged a jittery sell-off just before the close, erasing late-afternoon gains made on a well-received five-year Treasury note auction. The contract stopped just short of major support at 111-17, a double bottom from last week.
Analysts noted the contract has struggled to maintain gains above 112-00.
"It seems there has been a definite change in the tone of the market in the past week," said Jim Florsheim, senior vice president for ABN Amro Chicago Corp.
The 6.298 percent high yield and strong 3.19 bid-to-cover for the five-year issue should have been good news for the market, analysts said, but the gains proved fleeting.
"If you're long and you get numbers out just the way you like them, and the market can't rally, chances are we are not going to hold these levels," Florsheim said.
He said hedge fund selling has materialized in the past two sessions to cap forays above 112-00 in September bonds.

Debt futures began the session on a weak note following an overnight drop in dollar/yen sparked by a strong improvement in business sentiment in the Bank of Japan's quarterly Tankan survey, which fueled rate hike talk.
A 0.6 percent fall in U.S. durable goods orders in May, versus expectations for a 0.6 percent rise, provided some relief, but analysts said the report still showed underlying strength in the economy.
"Below the surface it was still a strong number, when you take out aircraft and defense," said Kathy Jones, futures analyst for Prudential Securities Inc.
Transportation orders, including aircraft and aircraft parts, were down 3.3 percent, and defense capital orders fell 12.8 percent.
Existing homes sales, also reported this morning, were strong at up 4.4 percent in May.

Overall, however, analysts said the data would have little impact on monetary policy when the Federal Open Market Committee meets next week. Fed policymakers are widely expected to leave short-term rates steady at the two-day meeting.
September bond futures ended 14/32 lower at 111-23, with September Treasury note futures off 6/32 at 108-11.
